description: Org-level data standards: naming conventions, surrogate keys, change-data-capture/audit, migrations, role tiers, and data-governance rules that apply to every project installing AI Agile.

standards.title: Every table has a corresponding change-data-capture (audit) table
standards.description: Every entity table (including join tables) has a corresponding change-data-capture table that mirrors the base table's columns and adds standard audit columns: an operation type (insert/update/delete), the time the row became active, the time it was superseded (null while current), and the acting user and session. The audit table is append-only history -- its mirrored columns carry no foreign-key constraints -- and is populated by an insert/update/delete trigger using a single shared capture function, not a bespoke per-table one. Exempt: the audit tables themselves and pure write-once append-only logging tables.
standards.rationale: A uniform per-table audit mirror gives every table a complete, attributable, append-only change history; a single shared capture function keeps it consistent.
acceptance_criteria: Each new entity table (except a write-once append-only log) in the diff has a matching change-data-capture table mirroring its columns plus the standard audit columns.
The audit table's mirrored columns carry no foreign-key constraints (it is append-only history).
Change capture is driven by an insert/update/delete trigger using the shared capture function, not a bespoke per-table one.
anti_patterns: Creating a new entity table with no corresponding change-data-capture table or trigger.

standards.title: Model many-to-many relationships with consistently-named join tables
standards.description: New many-to-many relationships use a join table whose name is formed from the two related entities in a fixed order (child before parent), joined by `_2_` -- e.g. `order_items_2_products` -- with columns carrying a shortened two-entity prefix. Its foreign-key columns reference the related tables' surrogate `{prefix}_id` keys. An array column is used for an association only as a deliberate, documented decision when it is never queried from the other side.
standards.rationale: A consistent join-table convention enables indexed lookups and foreign-key integrity from either side; array columns lose foreign keys, cascades, and reverse-side lookups.
acceptance_criteria: A new many-to-many relationship in the diff uses a `{child}_2_{parent}` join table (child before parent) with a shortened two-entity column prefix.
An array column is used for an association only when it is never queried from the other side, and that decision is recorded inline.
Join-table foreign-key columns reference the related tables' surrogate `{prefix}_id` primary keys.
anti_patterns: Adding an array column for a relationship that needs reverse-side lookups.

standards.title: Entity tables carry the core columns {prefix}_id, {prefix}_code, {prefix}_name, {prefix}_state
standards.description: Every column is prefixed with the table's singular entity name (e.g. `order_id`, `order_status`). Every entity base table carries the four core columns: `{prefix}_id` (surrogate primary key, see DATA-008), `{prefix}_code` (short unique code), `{prefix}_name` (display name), and `{prefix}_state` (lifecycle/status). Optional standard columns use conventional `{prefix}_` names where present (e.g. `{prefix}_description`, `{prefix}_order`). Join and audit tables are exempt from the core set.
standards.rationale: A guaranteed core set (id/code/name/state) lets lookups, display, and lifecycle handling work uniformly across every entity; missing core columns force per-entity special cases.
acceptance_criteria: Every new entity base table in the diff has `{prefix}_id`, `{prefix}_code`, `{prefix}_name`, and `{prefix}_state` columns.
All columns on a new table in the diff are prefixed with the entity's singular name (no bare `name`/`code`/`state`).
Optional standard columns in the diff use the conventional `{prefix}_` names.
anti_patterns: An entity table missing a `{prefix}_code`, `{prefix}_name`, or `{prefix}_state` column, or a bare unprefixed column name.

standards.title: Tables use a surrogate primary key named {prefix}_id
standards.description: Every table has a single surrogate primary key -- a system-generated, business-meaningless identifier -- named `{prefix}_id`, where `{prefix}` is the table's singular entity name (e.g. an `orders` table's key is `order_id`), placed as the table's first column and generated automatically. The primary-key constraint is named consistently (`{table}_pkey`). Join tables key on the shortened two-entity id; audit tables key on their own audit id.
standards.rationale: A uniform surrogate primary key keeps identity stable and business-meaning-free, avoids composite/natural-key churn, and keeps foreign keys simple and uniform.
acceptance_criteria: Each new table in the diff has a single surrogate primary key named `{prefix}_id`, placed as the first column and auto-generated.
No new primary key in the diff is a bare `id` or a composite natural key.
The primary-key constraint is named consistently (`{table}_pkey`).
anti_patterns: Using `id serial primary key` or a composite natural key instead of a surrogate `{prefix}_id`.

standards.title: Foreign keys are role-named with the owning-entity prefix
standards.description: Foreign-key columns are named for their semantic role within the owning entity, prefixed with the owning entity's name -- e.g. `order_customer`, `order_ship_address` -- not `{target}_id`. Self-referential foreign keys follow the same rule (e.g. `category_parent`). Each foreign key references the target's surrogate `{prefix}_id` primary key and its constraint is named consistently (`{table}_{column}_fkey`). Join-table foreign-key columns use the shortened two-entity prefix.
standards.rationale: Role-named foreign keys make each relationship self-describing and disambiguate multiple references to the same target, which a bare `{target}_id` cannot.
acceptance_criteria: New foreign-key columns in the diff are named `{owning_prefix}_{role}` for their semantic role, not `{target}_id`.
Each foreign key in the diff references the target table's `{prefix}_id` primary key, and the constraint is named `{table}_{column}_fkey`.
Self-referential foreign keys use a role suffix (e.g. `_parent`); join-table foreign keys use the two-entity prefix.
anti_patterns: Naming an order's customer foreign key `customer_id` instead of `order_customer`.

standards.title: Migrations are timestamped, forward-only, and self-contained
standards.description: Every schema change is a timestamped migration file (filename ordering defines apply order), applied forward-only: an applied migration is never rewritten; a mistake is corrected by a new migration -- never a manual/dashboard change or dump-and-restore. A migration that creates a table includes, in the same file, its change-data-capture table and trigger and its record-level access-control policies. Data/backfill migrations are separate from schema migrations and guarded by transaction boundaries.
standards.rationale: Forward-only timestamped migrations are the single source of schema truth and the basis of safe, drift-free deploys; a rewritten or partial migration breaks reproducibility.
acceptance_criteria: Each schema change in the diff is a new timestamped migration file, not an edit to an already-applied migration.
A migration that creates a table in the diff includes its change-data-capture table and trigger and its record-level access-control policies in the same file.
Backfill/data logic in the diff is in a separate migration from schema changes and is transaction-guarded.
anti_patterns: Editing an already-applied migration to fix it instead of adding a new corrective migration.

standards.title: Do not store regulated or PII data without ADR approval
standards.description: Regulated or personally-identifiable information (PII) -- financial, payment-card, health, government-identifier, biometric, or other special-category personal data -- is not stored unless a project ADR explicitly approves capturing that specific data and defines its handling. Absent an approving ADR, new columns and entities hold only non-regulated business or operational data. Approved sensitive attributes carry an explicit classification.
standards.rationale: Regulated/PII data brings compliance obligations (lawful basis, retention, access control, deletion, breach handling) that must be deliberately accepted, not incurred by accident.
acceptance_criteria: No new column or entity in the diff stores regulated or PII data unless a project ADR authorising that specific data is referenced.
Where such data is introduced under an approving ADR, the diff cites the ADR and applies the handling and classification it specifies.
Sensitive attributes added in the diff carry an explicit classification.
anti_patterns: Adding a column for personal/financial/health/government-id data with no approving ADR (e.g. a national-insurance number or card number).

standards.title: Database objects follow one consistent naming shape
standards.description: Database naming follows a single predictable shape: tables are named in plural snake_case (e.g. `orders`, `order_items`); every column is prefixed with the singular form of the table's entity name (`order_items` -> `item_id`, `item_name`); the primary key is the first column, named `{prefix}_id` (DATA-008); foreign keys are role-named with the owning-entity prefix and no `_id` suffix (DATA-009). Objects are grouped into schemas/namespaces by module, kept to the minimum.
standards.rationale: A single predictable naming shape lets a reader infer an object's entity, ownership, and relationships from its name alone, and keeps the schema legible.
acceptance_criteria: New tables in the diff are named in plural snake_case.
Every column on a new table in the diff is prefixed with the singular form of the table's entity name.
Primary-key and foreign-key naming in the diff follow DATA-008 and DATA-009.
anti_patterns: A singular table name (`order_item`) instead of the plural (`order_items`).

standards.title: Database roles follow the pattern {module}_{tier}
standards.description: Application database roles follow the pattern `{module}_{tier}`, where `module` is the application module and `tier` is one of the fixed access tiers: `_ro` (read-only), `_rw` (read-write), `_ad` (admin: create/delete/configure), `_wf` (workflow engine) -- e.g. `billing_ro`, `billing_rw`, `billing_ad`. Write policies check a write-capable role; read access uses the read-only role or an authenticated read policy. Roles are kept minimal: no ad-hoc names, no per-table roles, and no new tier beyond the established set without a deliberate decision.
standards.rationale: A consistent `{module}_{tier}` role taxonomy keeps access-control policies, entitlements, and grants legible and auditable per module and per tier; ad-hoc or per-table roles become unmanageable.
acceptance_criteria: New database roles in the diff are named `{module}_{ro|rw|wf|ad}`.
Write (insert/update/delete) policies in the diff require a write-capable role; read access uses the read-only role or an authenticated read policy.
No diff introduces a role outside the `{module}_{tier}` pattern, a per-table role, or a new tier without a recorded decision.
anti_patterns: A role named `editors` or `admin` instead of `{module}_rw` / `{module}_ad`.
